Key Takeaways

Oracle stock fell 12% in the past month (through Monday's close), mostly on three days of AI debt fears, while the S&P 500 rose 0.6%.

Nothing changed at the company, which still expects at least $90 billion of revenue in fiscal 2027, but investors are now pricing its $169.1 billion of debt.

S&P rates Oracle BBB-, the lowest investment-grade rating, and a downgrade to junk is the main risk to watch.

At 15x forward earnings, well below its 5-year average of 21x, Oracle looks like a buy for investors who can live with that credit risk.

Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) stock is down 12% in the past month (through Monday's close), while the S&P 500 rose 0.6%.

Almost none of that came from Oracle itself. The scare started in the bond market at CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ), down 25% over the same stretch, and spread to the company with far more debt riding on AI.

A credit scare that started at CoreWeave

On Thursday, Oct. 8, Oracle fell 5.5% as AI stocks sank on new details of OpenAI's revenue. That morning, Oracle was reportedly in talks with Apollo Global Management (APO:NYSE) and Goldman Sachs (GS:NYSE) to finance a big AI chip purchase, which put its debt back in the spotlight.

The worst day was Wednesday, Oct. 14, down 8.8%. September's inflation came in hot at 3.7%, reviving bets on Fed rate hikes, and one of CoreWeave's bonds yielded close to 15%.

On Thursday, the cost of insuring CoreWeave's debt against default hit a record, according to ICE Data Services. Some of its bonds slipped into distressed territory on Friday, and Oracle fell another 4.6%.

Oracle's debt is the whole story

Over the five fiscal years to May 2025, Oracle's total debt climbed to $109 billion while its cash fell from $46.6 billion to $11.2 billion.

Oracle (ORCL): total debt vs. cash and short-term investments, $ billions, fiscal 2021–2025 (years to May) (TIKR)

And by August 2026, debt was up to $169.1 billion, against $37.1 billion of cash.

In the August quarter, capex hit $28.5 billion, free cash flow was negative $5 billion, and Oracle sold $20 billion of new stock to help pay for the build. Interest expense rose 55% to $1.43 billion, outpacing the 31% growth in non-GAAP operating income, so rates now reach Oracle's earnings.

S&P cut Oracle to BBB- in July, the lowest investment-grade rating. That's what separates it from CoreWeave, whose bonds are high-yield. But Oracle's credit default swaps are priced more like BB and B credit, CNBC reported Monday.

The business hasn't flinched

Meanwhile, the business is humming. In the August quarter, revenue rose 30% to $19.3 billion, cloud infrastructure revenue jumped 121%, and the contracted backlog hit $664 billion. Management still expects at least $90 billion of revenue and $8.10 of non-GAAP EPS in fiscal 2027.

title: What Is Oracle’s (ORCL) Economic Moat, and Is It Widening or Narrowing?
detail:
What Is Oracle’s (ORCL) Economic Moat, and Is It Widening or Narrowing?
Suraj Santlani
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 7:43 AM MST 3 min read
ORCL
SPY
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

A moat is usually tested by asking what a customer would have to do to leave. For Oracle Corporation (NYSE:ORCL) that question has two answers now, and they point in opposite directions. The stock closed at $129.59 on October 19. It has returned -27% over the last 6 months, compared to an 11.6% return for the Insider Monkey Billionaire Index and 8.7% for the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust.

The database business is one of the stickiest franchises in software. The newer business is renting out computing capacity, and the test there is whether anyone can tell one rented server from another.

READ ALSO: 10 Most Undervalued Quality Stocks to Invest In

What Is Oracle's (ORCL) Economic Moat, and Is It Widening or Narrowing?
The Part Nobody Can Copy:

Moving a production database is the kind of project a company does once a decade. The data has to be migrated, the applications rewritten against a different dialect, and the whole thing proven before anyone switches over.

That shows up in what the business earns. It keeps 35.63% of revenue as operating profit and returns 41.19% on equity, which is not what a supplier earns when the customer has an easy alternative.

Oracle appears in our 10 Most Promising Cloud Stocks According to Hedge Funds, where it is the most widely held name. To see the rest, click HERE.

The Part Anyone Can Copy:

Renting computing capacity is a different trade. The customer is buying a commodity, the contract is usually shorter, and the competition includes three of the largest technology companies in the world.

It also costs a great deal to enter. Borrowings come to 251.72% of equity, and over the past year the company spent far more building capacity than the whole business produced in cash, funding the gap with debt. A moat that has to be bought each year is a different thing from one already dug.

Which way the moat is moving depends on which half grows. Revenue added 29.60% in the latest quarter, and the capacity side is the one absorbing the spending.

DON'T MISS: 10 Best Fundamental Stocks to Invest in According to Billionaires

What the Price Says About It:

At 17.76 times what analysts expect next year, the shares are cheap for a company adding revenue at this rate. The stock has fallen 27.8% over six months while the market rose.

That gap is the argument in one line. Either the market is wrong about how much of the old moat carries into the new business, or it has worked out that the new business does not have one.

Technology stocks came under pressure last week as concerns about AI financing and spending weighed on investor sentiment. The sell-off hit major AI infrastructure players and pushed both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite into negative territory for the week.

AI infrastructure providers CoreWeave CRWV and Nebius NBIS each ended the week down more than 25%. Both companies, along with Oracle ORCL, are facing questions about their ability to generate free cash flow (read: AI Debt Boom: ETF Areas to Play).

Baird technology strategist Ted Mortonson told Yahoo Finance that these companies are likely among the weakest in the tech sector in terms of free cash flow. He also highlighted the rising cost of capital amid inflation worries and growing scrutiny of the financial arrangements supporting the AI boom.

Chip Industry Signals Point to Strong AI Demand

While AI infrastructure stocks struggled, comments from semiconductor equipment maker ASML ASML and contract chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. TSM offered a more encouraging picture of underlying demand (read: TSMC's Record Q3 Earnings & Upbeat Outlook Put These ETFs in Focus).

Their commentary suggests that demand for AI chips and related infrastructure remains robust, even as investors grow more cautious about how companies finance their expansion and convert spending into profits.

UBS strategists similarly viewed the latest volatility as a recalibration of expectations rather than a fundamental break in the AI investment story, as quoted on Yahoo Finance (read: Buy the Dip in Semiconductor Stocks & ETFs?).

Earnings Growth Matters

Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, UBS's chief investment officer of the Americas and global head of equities, advised investors to focus on companies where AI spending is translating into sustainable earnings growth and wider adoption across businesses and consumers, as quoted on the same Yahoo Finance article.

Investors will now be watching to see whether massive AI investments can generate durable profits and justify the valuations attached to AI-related stocks.

Debt-funded AI cloud providers are back under pressure as concerns about borrowing costs spread across the group. First of all, CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) shares are down 4% to $58.67 in morning trading.

Andriy Onufriyenko / Moment via Getty Images

Moreover, Nebius Group (NASDAQ:NBIS) shares are falling harder, down 5% to $162.20. However, Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) stock is only down 0.52% to $128.95, a comparatively steady contrast to the slide in CoreWeave and Nebius shares.

That split shows strain concentrated in the most debt-reliant corner of AI infrastructure, where CoreWeave and Nebius both operate. With its far broader revenue base, Oracle stock sits outside the worst of the selling.

HSBC Doubles Down on Its Reduce Call

HSBC repeated its Reduce rating on CoreWeave in a note on Monday. The accompanying price target sits well below where CoreWeave shares last closed, leaving little doubt about the direction of that call.

CoreWeave's central challenge is revenue per megawatt of capacity, which could trail what larger cloud providers earn. Those bigger rivals offer broader services. They serve more diversified customers, giving them more ways to make money from each data center they run. Scale matters here, because bigger platforms can spread their costs across many products.

Two more pressure points weigh on CoreWeave. Slower growth at AI model developers could soften demand for short-term capacity, and rising borrowing costs make new infrastructure harder to finance.

Oracle Bonds Face Downgrade Risks As AI Trade Fizzles Across Tech Sector ©@yhelfman via Canva, @Yurich84 from Getty Images via Canva
Key Stats for Oracle Stock

Price change for Oracle stock in last 6 months: -27%

$ORCL Stock Price as of Oct. 19: $130

52-Week High: $287

$ORCL Stock Price Target: $237

What Happened?

Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) is facing fresh worries in the bond market. Much of the AI trade cooled last week, led by CoreWeave, whose stock and debt have both been falling. Oracle is still investment grade, but its loans are starting to trade like high-yield debt.

The clearest sign is in credit default swaps, which work like insurance against default. Oracle's five-year spread hit 300 basis points on Thursday before settling at 295.

S&P Global Market Intelligence says that level lines up with BB and B credit, which is junk territory. S&P cut Oracle to BBB- in July.

It said the fast-growing infrastructure business is adding credit risk. Another downgrade could come if leverage stays above 4x, or if Oracle doesn't look on track for positive free operating cash flow by fiscal 2029.

The cash numbers explain the concern. Oracle has issued $118 billion in long-term debt and has another $39 billion in capital and lease obligations.

Analysts expect free cash flow of -$23.7 billion this year and -$36 billion in 2027. Part of this spending supports a $300 billion deal with OpenAI.

ORCL Stock Revenue, EBIT and Free Cash Flow Estimates in Billion USD (TIKR)

Oracle's latest quarter was strong.

Revenue hit $19.3 billion, up 30%.

Cloud infrastructure revenue rose 121% to $7.4 billion.

Non-GAAP EPS climbed 30% to $1.92.

Oracle also raised its full-year outlook to at least $90 billion in revenue and $8.10 in EPS.

Cash is still going out the door, though. Capital spending was $28 billion in the quarter, which left free cash flow at negative $5 billion.

Oracle expects $90 billion to $95 billion in capex for the full year.

What the Market Is Telling Us About Oracle Stock

The bond market is asking how long Oracle can fund this buildout, and a move to junk would matter beyond Oracle.

Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid says it could force investors who can only hold investment-grade debt to sell. Oracle is also seen as a bellwether for AI, so the effects could spread.

A junk rating would also raise Oracle's borrowing costs. Jamie Meyers of Laffer Tengler, which owns Oracle stock, says high-yield buyers won't take 30-year debt.

He still isn't worried and says Oracle just needs time to finish its buildout.

Vanguard's Brad Collins agrees. He says balance sheets are healthy and he wouldn't apply the stress in high yield to investment-grade names.

Oracle says keeping its investment-grade rating is its first priority and also expects strong free cash flow once projects ramp up.
